editorial_reason: Read Stacks 9.13, Lemmas 9.13.1 and 9.13.3. They explicitly treat characters as multiplicative monoid homomorphisms to a field and show distinct characters are linearly independent as functions. The term heading itself is a theorem, so I retain the mathematical object rather than mistaking the independence result for a separate definition.

definitions.text: For a monoid G and a field L, an L-valued multiplicative character of G is a homomorphism from G to the multiplicative monoid of L; in particular it sends the identity of G to 1 and respects multiplication.
definitions.context_hint: Algebra: field-valued multiplicative character of a monoid

editorial_reason: Read Stacks 9.26, Definitions 9.26.1, 9.26.4 and 9.26.9. The section explicitly presents several distinct objects and properties concerning transcendence, and a relative closure notion within a specified extension field.

definitions.text: A family (x_i) of elements of a field extension K/k is algebraically independent over k when the evaluation homomorphism k[X_i:i∈I]→K, sending each indeterminate X_i to x_i, is injective.
definitions.context_hint: Field theory: algebraic independence over a base field

definitions.text: An extension K/k is purely transcendental if it is isomorphic as an extension of k to the field of rational functions in an arbitrary set of algebraically independent indeterminates over k.
A transcendence basis B of K over k is an algebraically independent subset B⊆K for which every element of K is algebraic over the subfield k(B) generated by k and B.
The transcendence degree trdeg_k(K) of a field extension K/k is the cardinality of any transcendence basis of K over k, independent of the particular basis chosen.

For a field extension K/k, the algebraic closure of k inside K is the intermediate subfield consisting of all elements of K that are algebraic over k; this is a relative, not necessarily algebraically closed, field.
definitions.context_hint: Field theory: relative algebraic closure inside an extension

definitions.text: Given K/k, the base field k is algebraically closed in K when every element of K algebraic over k already belongs to k; equivalently, its relative algebraic closure in K equals k.
definitions.context_hint: Field theory: relatively algebraically closed subfield

editorial_reason: Read Stacks 10.129, especially Theorem 10.129.4 defining and proving openness for the set of primes at which the localized S-module is flat over the base ring R. This is a precise 'flat locus' within Spec(S) for a specified ring map and module.

definitions.text: Given a ring homomorphism R→S and an S-module M, its flat locus relative to R is the subset of Spec(S) consisting of primes q for which the localization M_q is flat as an R-module, equivalently as an R_p-module for p=q∩R.
definitions.context_hint: Commutative algebra: flat locus of an S-module over a base ring

editorial_reason: Read Stacks 4.25, Lemma 4.25.1. Although the heading is a representability criterion, the source explicitly describes a representable covariant functor via a natural identification with an outgoing Hom functor.

definitions.text: A covariant functor F:C→Sets is representable if there exists an object X of C together with a natural isomorphism F(Y)≅Hom_C(X,Y) for every object Y in C.
definitions.context_hint: Category theory: covariant set-valued representable functor

editorial_reason: Read Stacks 3.9 introductory paragraphs, which explicitly define a cardinal-valued size of a scheme to control small subcategories and state a set-theoretic boundedness lemma. This is a defined size invariant, not an invented notion of a category of schemes.

definitions.text: The size of a scheme S in the Stacks Project's set-theoretic convention is max(aleph_0,κ_1,κ_2), where κ_1 counts affine open subsets of S and κ_2 is the supremum of cardinalities of their rings of global sections.
definitions.context_hint: Set theory and algebraic geometry: cardinal size of a scheme

editorial_reason: Read Stacks 10.134, Definition 10.134.1 and the canonical presentation preceding it. The naive cotangent complex is a specific two-term S-module complex, with the map induced by the universal derivation, not simply the module of Kähler differentials.

definitions.text: For a ring map R→S, let P=R[X_s:s∈S] map canonically onto S and put I=ker(P→S). The naive cotangent complex NL_{S/R} is the two-term complex I/I²→Ω_{P/R}⊗_P S, with I/I² in homological degree 1 and the induced differential from universal derivation.
definitions.context_hint: Commutative algebra: naive cotangent complex of a ring homomorphism

editorial_reason: Read Stacks 10.46, particularly Lemmas 10.46.1, 10.46.3 and 10.46.4. The source discusses ring maps whose induced maps on prime spectra are homeomorphisms after arbitrary base changes; this stable notion is the universal homeomorphism of spectra.

definitions.text: A homomorphism of commutative rings R→S induces a universal homeomorphism on spectra if for every R-algebra R′ the canonical map Spec(S⊗_R R′)→Spec(R′) is a homeomorphism.
definitions.context_hint: Commutative algebra: universal homeomorphism induced by a ring map

editorial_reason: Read Stacks 10.106, which explicitly refers to its defining Definition 10.60.10. Followed that link and verified the equality between Krull dimension and minimal number of generators of the maximal ideal, retaining the Noetherian local hypothesis.

definitions.text: A Noetherian local ring (R,m) of Krull dimension d is regular local if m can be generated by d elements; equivalently dim_{R/m}(m/m²)=d.
definitions.source_section: Definition 10.60.10 (00KU), referenced at start of Section 10.106
definitions.context_hint: Commutative algebra: regular Noetherian local ring

definitions.text: In a regular Noetherian local ring (R,m) of dimension d, a regular system of parameters is a d-element sequence in m that generates the maximal ideal m.
definitions.context_hint: Commutative algebra: regular system of parameters

editorial_reason: Read Stacks 10.124, 'Applications of Zariski's Main Theorem'. The content is a sequence of lemmas applying previously defined notions of quasi-finiteness, order and finite maps, rather than the introduction of a distinct definition called 'applications of Zariski's Main Theorem'. Source links to earlier defining sections remain possible research leads.

Read Stacks 10.81, Lemma 10.81.1 and Lazard's theorem 10.81.4. The source supplies a valid equivalent characterization of module flatness using filtered colimits of finite free modules, which is kept as an alternative mathematical formulation rather than confused with a separate kind of flatness.

definitions.text: An R-module M is flat if and only if M is a filtered colimit of finite-rank free R-modules; this is Lazard's equivalent characterization of the usual exactness-preservation definition of flatness.
definitions.context_hint: Commutative algebra: flat module, filtered-colimit characterization

editorial_reason: Read Stacks 10.66, Definition 10.66.1 and Lemma 10.66.2. The weakly associated prime condition uses minimal primes over an element's annihilator, which is distinct from requiring the prime to equal the annihilator itself.

definitions.text: For an R-module M, a prime ideal p of R is weakly associated to M if some element m∈M has p among the prime ideals minimal over its annihilator Ann_R(m).
definitions.context_hint: Commutative algebra: weakly associated prime ideal of a module

editorial_reason: Read Stacks 26.7, Lemma 26.7.1 and the introductory recall of the quasi-coherent-sheaf definition. On affine schemes the construction from an R-module via localizations gives the correct precise characterization.

definitions.text: On X=Spec(R), a quasi-coherent O_X-module is an O_X-module isomorphic to the sheaf ~M associated with some R-module M; for every standard open D(f), the sections of ~M on D(f) identify with the localization M_f.
definitions.context_hint: Algebraic geometry: quasi-coherent sheaf on an affine scheme
